name_en: Doi Mae Salong Oolong No. 17 (Thai Ruan Zhi)
name_native: ชาอู่หลงเบอร์ 17
origin_region: Chiang Rai · Mae Fa Luang · Doi Mae Salong (Santikhiri), also Doi Wawee and Doi Tung
cultivar: Thai 'No. 17', sold as Ruan Zhi; a Taiwanese cultivar introduced from Taiwan (TTES No. 17 Bai Lu in Taiwanese numbering)
processing: Ball-rolled green-style oolong in the Taiwanese manner: withered, bruised, lightly oxidised (around 15–25%), pan-fired, rolled in cloth into tight balls and dried; usually unroasted, with lightly roasted and more oxidised 'red' versions made from the same bushes.
harvest_season: Several picks a year; winter (November to January) and spring (March to April) harvests give the cleanest, most floral tea.
appearance_dry: Tight, slightly lighter and smaller jade-green pellets than No. 12, with stems, and a high, fresh floral scent.
appearance_liquor: Very pale yellow-green, bright and clear.
appearance_wet: Whole thin leaves with stems, bright green and tender.
taste_profile: Light and lifted: orchid and fresh-cut flowers, a hint of green apple, a thinner, crisper body than No. 12 and a clean, sweet, slightly cooling finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse, then keep the water just below the boil and the steeps short; it is more delicate than No. 12 and turns grassy if overbrewed. Also a fine cold brew.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's harvest, vacuum-packed in 100–200 g foil, labelled 'No. 17' with the farm and sometimes the season; winter and spring lots are the premium. Drink within a year, keep sealed and cool. Roasted or red-oolong versions from the same cultivar keep longer and are sold without a vintage.
description:
No. 17 is the other number on the shop signs of Doi Mae Salong, and the lighter, more floral of the village's two main oolongs. The Thai hills call the cultivar Ruan Zhi, 'soft stem', and sell it under the Taiwanese extension number 17; the naming is tangled, since in Taiwan No. 17 is the cultivar Bai Lu and 'soft stem' usually refers to Qing Xin, but in Thailand the number is what counts, and every farm in Mae Salong, Doi Wawee and the Doi Tung project grows it.

It is processed the same way as No. 12, bruised, lightly oxidised and rolled into tight green balls, but the leaf is thinner and the character very different: where No. 12 is creamy, No. 17 is high and floral, closer in spirit to a light Taiwanese high-mountain tea. The cool-season harvests, picked in the dry months from November to April, are clearly better than the rainy-season ones.

The cup is orchid and fresh flowers with a hint of green apple, a crisp, fairly light body and a clean sweet finish that cools in the throat. It is a tea for short steeps and attention; brewed too hot or too long it goes thin and grassy. From the same bushes the better farms also make a lightly roasted version and a more oxidised 'red oolong', which are worth trying if the green style feels too light.

It is sold vacuum-packed by farm and harvest, at the village and in the cities, usually just as 'Oolong No. 17'. Prices are a fraction of Taiwanese high-mountain tea, and it is often what fills cheap 'Taiwan oolong' packs elsewhere; buying it under its own name from a named Thai farm is both more honest and better value. Ask for winter tea.

Try No. 12 and No. 17 from the same farm side by side, then a Four Seasons (Si Ji Chun) if they have it: three Taiwanese cultivars, one Thai mountain, and a clear lesson in what the bush contributes.
sources_note: Cultivar identity is the main uncertainty: Thai 'No. 17 / Ruan Zhi' is sold as one cultivar, while Taiwanese numbering gives No. 17 as Bai Lu and 'Ruan Zhi' as a name for Qing Xin. The card describes the Thai product as sold and flags the confusion.
